title: Moses is rebuked
hook: a voice tells Moses he was sent to join people to God, not to part them (Masnavi 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses scolded a shepherd for offering to comb God's hair, and the shepherd walked off into the desert. Your line was in your own words. Did you say thanks plainly? Day one hundred ninety-five.

Maybe you've been corrected at a moment you were trying your hardest. You cooked for someone and they told you how their mother makes it. You finally opened up about something and got a lecture back. The correction might even have been right. But something closed, and it didn't open again for a long time. Yesterday a shepherd poured out his heart, got corrected by a prophet, and left. Moses, presumably, walked on feeling he'd done his job. Then he hears a voice, and it isn't pleased with him. Today: Moses is rebuked.
screen: `CORRECTED WHILE TRYING YOUR HARDEST.` → `SOMETHING CLOSED.` → `MOSES IS REBUKED.`

segments.voice: In Rumi's telling, a revelation comes to Moses from God, and it goes something like this. You have parted my servant from me. Did you come as a prophet to bring people together, or to split them apart? Rumi puts it in a pair of rhyming lines that Persian speakers still quote: you came to unite, not to sever. Then the voice goes on. I have given every person a way of their own, a way of speaking. What is praise from him would be blame from you. What's honey for one is poison for another. And then Rumi's most famous twist. The voice says: I don't look at the tongue and the words. I look at the heart and its state. Rumi gives an example from his own world: the idiom of India is praise for the people of India, the idiom of Sind for the people of Sind. Different words, the same longing. Notice what the story doesn't say. It doesn't say Moses was wrong that God has no body. Rumi's tradition keeps that teaching. It says Moses was wrong to make the shepherd's words the test of his heart. The man's language was mistaken. His love was not. That's hard for anyone who loves getting things right, and most religious people do, in every tradition. The story isn't against correct teaching. It's a warning about what correction can cost when it lands on someone who is only trying to love. So when you hear someone pray or talk about the sacred in a way that isn't yours, the story suggests a first thought: their words, not mine. Your line.
screen: `YOU HAVE PARTED MY SERVANT FROM ME.` · `YOU CAME TO UNITE, NOT TO SEVER.` · `I LOOK AT THE HEART, NOT THE TONGUE.` · then, large: `THEIR WORDS, NOT MINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to someone's way of praying. Settle, and bring to mind someone whose way with the sacred is different from yours. A grandmother with her beads, a friend who talks to the universe, a colleague who fasts, a child at bedtime. Picture them in the middle of it. Don't correct anything, even inside. Just listen for the heart underneath the words. The bell holds the time.
Moses is rebuked. A voice tells Moses he was sent to join people to God, not to part them, and that God looks at the heart, not the tongue. Today's word.
Your line: their words, not mine. Today, when you hear something said about God or meaning that isn't how you'd say it, think the line before you think anything else. Day one hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Readers of Rumi often cite this story when they talk about respecting other people's ways of prayer, and many Sufi teachers use it to warn against judging sincerity by vocabulary.

match.prompt: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
pairs: praise for the people of Sind

myth: the story says Moses was wrong that God has no body
Rumi keeps that teaching. Moses was wrong to judge the shepherd's heart by his words.
the voice says what's praise from one may be blame from another
every person is given their own way of speaking.
the rebuke comes from the shepherd
it comes to Moses as a revelation from God.

fork.setup: you're Moses. you've just corrected a shepherd's prayer, and a voice from God asks you why. what does the voice say you were sent to do?
options: to bring people together with God, not split them apart.
fork.reveal: you came to unite, not to sever. the rhyming lines are still quoted in Persian today.

original.note: Persian, from Arabic: union, joining. 'you came to join (vasl), not to sever (fasl).'

trapdoor: what you thought: God tells Moses off for being strict.
what it means: God looks at the heart, not the words, and a prophet is sent to join people to God.
what a scholar hears: the famous couplet on vasl and fasl, union and severance, and Rumi's image of each people praising in its own idiom, India's for India, Sind's for Sind.

sources.ref: Masnavi Book 2, after 2.1720 (God's rebuke of Moses)

notes: Paraphrased from Nicholson: 'you have parted my servant from me', 'did you come to unite or to sever', 'every one a way of his own', praise/blame, honey/poison, 'I look not at the tongue and speech, I look at the inward spirit and state', the idiom of Hind and of Sind. Confirm each and their order.
Persian couplet: 'tu barāye vasl kardan āmadī / nay barāye fasl kardan āmadī'. Confirm transliteration and that vasl is spelled وصل.
The script avoids the nearby line about 'the religion of love' being apart from all religions, to keep clear of comparing traditions. Keeper may decide whether to mention it.
'Most religious people do, in every tradition' is meant warmly, not as a judgment. Confirm tone.
